book_understanding.teaching_order: A textbook defines nominal GDP (current prices) and real GDP (constant prices), then gives the deflator formula. Here the video first settles last video's question, re-states that factor cost is the better production indicator, and then breaks that belief: with one laptop a year and 10% inflation, GDP still rises every year. Only after the learner sees GDP rise with no extra output are the names given (inflated, then nominal; remove the inflation, then real). The method follows the same laptop back along a year line to a base year, the deflator is the tool that does it, and the four-way tree comes last as a summary.
book_understanding.breakdown_rule: Hold one quantity fixed (one laptop a year) and let only price move, so every new term is the name for what that one change does to GDP.

opening.what: Recalls last video: which is the better indicator of whether production is rising, factor cost or market price; factor cost, since market price also rises with taxes; India switched to market price in 2015 (question card and a 15K-flat vs rising market-price table).

moves.concept: factor cost vs market price as a production indicator (recall)
moves.what: Factor cost is the better production indicator, because market price can rise just from higher taxes; yet India moved to market price in 2015 (gap words recovered by re-transcription).

moves.concept: why India switched to market price in 2015
moves.what: Last video I asked you why the change was made; here is the answer.

moves.concept: why India switched to market price in 2015
moves.what: To match global practice: major economies measure GDP at market price, so measuring ours the same way makes growth comparable with developed countries.

moves.concept: why India switched to market price in 2015
moves.what: In 2008 the UN System of National Accounts also recommended market price for India.

moves.concept: why India switched to market price in 2015
moves.what: Names three viewers who answered last video's question correctly (a viewer shout-out; none of the listed moves fits exactly).

moves.concept: inflation raises factor-cost GDP with no extra output
moves.what: As we said, factor cost is the better indicator of whether production is rising.

moves.concept: inflation raises factor-cost GDP with no extra output
moves.what: But that does not mean factor cost rises only when production rises; the reason is inflation.

moves.concept: inflation raises factor-cost GDP with no extra output
moves.what: 'Maan lijiye': one laptop a year, 10,000 in 2020; inflation 10%, yaani everything 10% dearer each year, so 11,000 in 2021 and 12,100 in 2022; GDP equals those values.

moves.concept: inflation raises factor-cost GDP with no extra output
moves.what: GDP rose every year though goods and services did not increase at all; yaani this is inflated GDP.

moves.concept: nominal GDP vs real GDP
moves.what: Yaani inflation is already added inside this GDP.

moves.concept: nominal GDP vs real GDP
moves.what: GDP with inflation added is nominal GDP: current prices times quantities. Take the inflation out and it becomes real GDP.

moves.concept: removing inflation back to a base year
moves.what: But how is inflation taken out? How is real GDP calculated?

moves.concept: removing inflation back to a base year
moves.what: Back to the example: remove one year's inflation from 12,100 and you get 11,000; remove another and you get 10,000.

moves.concept: removing inflation back to a base year
moves.what: So how many years of inflation must be removed?

moves.concept: removing inflation back to a base year
moves.what: Every economy has a base year, and inflation is removed back to it; India's base year is FY 2012.

moves.concept: removing inflation back to a base year
moves.what: In FY 2023, valuing all output at market price gives nominal GDP; with one laptop that is 12,100.

moves.concept: GDP deflator and the real GDP formula
moves.what: To get real GDP, remove all inflation since FY 2012; this is done by the GDP deflator.

moves.concept: GDP deflator and the real GDP formula
moves.what: Suppose the deflator is 10: real GDP = nominal GDP / deflator = 12,100 / 10 = 1,210.

moves.concept: GDP deflator and the real GDP formula
moves.what: The deflator lets the air out of nominal GDP ('hawa nikal deta hai'); a balloon goes flat on screen.

moves.concept: four ways of calculating GDP; India's choice
moves.what: So far: two kinds, real (constant prices, inflation removed) and nominal; each at factor cost or market price, so four ways.

moves.concept: four ways of calculating GDP; India's choice
moves.what: India calculates nominal GDP at market price; why market price was answered in this video.

moves.concept: four ways of calculating GDP; India's choice
moves.what: Write in the comments why India uses nominal and not real GDP; answer next video.

narration.density: About 15 terms (factor cost, market price, indirect taxes, subsidies, global practice, System of National Accounts, inflation, inflated GDP, nominal GDP, current prices, real GDP, base year, GDP deflator, constant prices, four ways) in about 410 s, about 2 per minute. talmel_summary: Picture and voice are almost always together, and in the core (115-350 s) the picture does the explaining: quantity stuck at 1 while the price climbs, dotted arrows carrying each price into GDP, the inflation stripe sliding out of the GDP block as 'Nominal' is struck and 'REAL' written, arcs hopping back to the base year, panels turning into the terms of the formula, and a balloon going flat for 'hawa nikalna'. The opening 100 s are weaker (text cards, a world map, viewer avatars). Two tiles (2, 8) fell in transcript gaps and were checked against a re-transcription.

voice.notes: About 161 words per minute, the slowest and most teacherly of this batch. First-person and dialogic: 'maine aapse poocha tha', 'main chahta hoon ki aap comment box mein likh ke bataiye'. Numbers are read in full rupees (dus hazaar, gyarah hazaar, barah hazaar ek sau) and the 10% is unpacked at once ('yaani har saal cheezein 10% mehngi'). Uses questions as pauses ('bat question ye hai...'). Ends on a colloquial image, 'hawa nikal deta hai'.

game_ideas.player_does: Runs a one-product economy for five years, setting how many laptops are made and the inflation rate each year.
game_ideas.process_happens: The table fills (quantity, price, GDP); the GDP block grows with a yellow inflation stripe; a second block shows real GDP at base-year prices.
game_ideas.win: Make real GDP grow three years in a row (more laptops), not just nominal GDP.
game_ideas.lose: Raising only inflation makes nominal GDP climb while real GDP stays flat; the 'inflated GDP' tag appears and the stripe fills the block.

game_ideas.player_does: Reads news-style claims ('GDP up 12%, so we made 12% more goods') with the year's inflation given, and taps the error.
game_ideas.process_happens: The stripe slides out of the GDP block, showing how much of the rise was inflation and how much was real; arcs hop back to the base year.
game_ideas.win: Correctly split each rise into inflation and real growth.
game_ideas.lose: Accepting the claim shows the stripe still inside the block and the real growth much smaller than claimed.
game_ideas.concept: removing inflation back to a base year

game_ideas.player_does: Places cards (real/nominal, factor cost/market price, constant/current prices, includes taxes/excludes) onto the four-leaf GDP tree.
game_ideas.process_happens: Each leaf fills; when all four are right, India's leaf (nominal at market price) lights with the 'kyun?' tag.
game_ideas.win: All four leaves correctly built and India's choice found.
game_ideas.lose: Putting 'constant prices' under nominal flashes the inflation stripe back into the block.

checks_learned: A worked formula result must agree with the running example it reuses (12,100 / 10 = 1,210 while the peel-back story landed on 10,000); a numeric consistency check should catch it.
When an index such as a deflator is used, its scale (base = 100) must be stated with the number.
Every derived cell in a table should be reached by an arrow from its source cell (done here; enforce).
When a term is transformed into another (nominal into real), strike the old word and write the new one at the moment the voice says it (done here; enforce).
Reasons given only as text cards for more than about 20 s (the 2015 switch) should be flagged for a picture.
BIE must not show real organisation emblems (UN flag) or invent viewer names for shout-outs.
Keep the varying quantity to one: holding output at 1 while price changes isolated the idea cleanly; a check can require one variable changing per numeric example.

teaching_best.why: A claim the learner just accepted (factor cost rises only with production) is shown, then stamped with a red cross: inflation opens the lesson.
Quantity stays 1 in every row while the laptop's price climbs 10K, 11K, 12.1K: GDP rises with nothing more made.
Inflation is a removable stripe inside the GDP block; it slides out, 'Nominal' is struck and 'REAL' written.
Dotted arcs hop back year by year along the line to a base year: 'how far back to remove inflation' is a picture.
The formula is built from the panels already on screen, then a balloon goes flat for 'hawa nikal deta hai'.

teaching_weak.why: About 40 s of text cards, a world map and a UN flag for the reason behind the 2015 switch.
About 15 s of viewer shout-out between the answer and the new topic.
'Deflator = 10' gives 1,210, which contradicts the peel-back story (10,000) and gives no scale for the deflator.
Ends on a typed list and an open question; no recap of what real vs nominal means for the learner.
